what_its_for: Fenoprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to relieve pain, swelling, and stiffness caused by arthritis (both rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis). It can also be used for mild to moderate pain relief from other conditions. It works by reducing the chemicals in your body that cause pain and inflammation.
how_to_take: Take fenoprofen by mouth with a full glass of water (8 ounces). To avoid stomach upset, take it with food, milk, or an antacid. Do not lie down for at least 10 minutes after taking this medicine. Swallow the capsules whole — do not crush or chew them. Take this medication exactly as directed by your doctor or pharmacist.
dosing: For arthritis, the usual adult dose is 400 mg to 600 mg taken 3 to 4 times a day. For general pain relief, the usual adult dose is 200 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Do not take more than 3,200 mg in one day unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Always follow the exact dose your doctor prescribed for you.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store fenoprofen at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medication out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medications down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of them.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking fenoprofen, as it increases your risk of stomach bleeding. Do not take aspirin or other NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen) unless your doctor tells you it is safe to do so. Avoid activities that may increase your risk of bleeding or injury. Be careful when driving or operating machinery, as this medication may sometimes cause dizziness. Limit prolonged sun exposure and wear sunscreen, as fenoprofen may make your skin more sensitive to sunlight.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience: chest pain, shortness of breath, sudden weakness or slurred speech (signs of a heart attack or stroke); black, tarry, or bloody stools, or vomiting blood (signs of stomach bleeding); severe stomach pain; swelling of the face, lips, throat, or tongue (allergic reaction); skin rash or blisters; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); dark urine or decreased urination; unusual weight gain or swelling in your legs or feet; or ringing in the ears or sudden hearing changes. Also call your doctor if your pain or swelling does not improve or gets worse.
when_it_works: You may start to feel some pain relief within the first few hours after taking a dose. However, for the full anti-inflammatory benefits — such as reduced swelling and stiffness from arthritis — it may take several days to a few weeks of regular use before you notice the most improvement. Keep taking it as prescribed even if you feel better.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and older) are at higher risk for stomach bleeding, kidney problems, and heart-related side effects. Use the lowest effective dose and check in with your doctor regularly. Pregnant women should avoid fenoprofen, especially during the last 3 months of pregnancy, as it can harm the unborn baby. Talk to your doctor before using it at any stage of pregnancy. It is not known if fenoprofen passes into breast milk; consult your doctor before breastfeeding. Fenoprofen is not approved for use in children under 18 years of age. Patients with kidney disease, liver disease, heart disease, or a history of stomach ulcers should use fenoprofen with caution and only under close medical supervision.
